first_draft_paragraphs.text: “That was a mighty good toast, Jane,” said Mr. Hersheimmer, as he and his cousin were being driven back in the Rolls-Royce to the _Ritz_. “You were just wonderful!”
Jane shook her head.
“I don’t feel wonderful. At heart I’m just tired and lonesome--and longing for my own country.”

“That brings me to something I wanted to say. I heard the Ambassador telling you his wife hoped you would come to them at the Embassy right away. That’s good enough, but I’ve got another plan. Jane--I want you to marry me! You can’t love me right away, of course. But I’ve loved you from the very moment I set eyes on your photo--and now I’ve seen you I’m simply crazy about you! You shall take your own time. Maybe you’ll never come to love me, and if that’s the case I’ll manage to set you free. But I want the right to look after you, and take care of you.”
“That’s what I want,” said the girl wistfully. “Some one who’ll be good to me.”
“Sure thing. Then I guess that’s all fixed up, and I’ll see the archbishop about a special license to-morrow morning.”
“Oh, Julius!”
“Well, I don’t want to hustle you any, Jane, but there’s no sense in waiting about.”
But a small hand was slipped into his.
“I love you now, Julius,” said Jane Finn. “I loved you that first moment in the car when the bullet grazed your cheek....”
Five minutes later Jane murmured softly:
“I don’t know London very well, Julius, but is it such a very long way from the _Savoy_ to the _Ritz?_”

“It depends how you go,” explained Julius unblushingly. “We’re going by way of Regent’s Park! Why, Jane, the only reason I had the supper at the _Savoy_ was so that I could drive you home. You and Tuppence have been sticking together like Siamese twins. I guess another day of it would have driven me and Beresford stark staring mad!”
“Oh. Is he----?”
“Of course he is. Head over ears.”
“I thought so,” said Jane thoughtfully.
“Why?”
“From all the things Tuppence didn’t say!”
“There you have me beat,” said Mr. Hersheimmer. But Jane only laughed.
In the meantime, the Young Adventurers were sitting bolt upright, very stiff and ill at ease, in a taxi which, with a singular lack of originality, was also returning to the _Ritz_ via Regent’s Park.
A terrible constraint seemed to have settled down between them. They were tongue-tied--paralysed. All the old _camaraderie_ was gone. At last Tuppence made a desperate effort.
“Rather fun, wasn’t it?”
“Rather.”
“I like Julius,” essayed Tuppence again.
Tommy was suddenly galvanized into life.
“You’re not going to marry him, do you hear?” he said dictatorially. “I forbid it.”
“Oh!” said Tuppence meekly. “He doesn’t want to marry me--he really only asked me out of kindness. He’s head over ears in love with Jane. I expect he’s proposing to her now.”
“She’ll do for him very nicely,” said Tommy condescendingly.
“But I suppose you prefer sterling worth,” said Tuppence demurely.
“I--oh, dash it all, Tuppence, you know!”

“I like your uncle, Tommy,” said Tuppence, hastily creating a diversion. “By the way, are you going to accept Mr. Carter’s offer of a Government job, or take a richly remunerated post in America on Julius’s ranch?”
“I shall stick to the old ship, I think. I feel you’d be more at home in London.”
“I don’t see where I come in.”
“I do,” said Tommy positively.
Tuppence stole a glance at him sideways.
“There’s the money, too,” she observed thoughtfully. “We’re going to get a cheque each. Mr. Carter told me so.”
“Did you ask how much?” inquired Tommy sarcastically.
“Yes,” said Tuppence triumphantly. “But I shan’t tell you.”
“Tuppence, you are the limit!”
“Well, shopping is almost as good as adventures,” said Tuppence dreamily. “Think of buying old furniture, and bright carpets, and a divan with lots of cushions.”
“Hold hard,” said Tommy. “What’s all this for?”
“Possibly a house--but I think a flat.”
“Whose flat?”
“You think I mind saying it, but I don’t in the least! _Ours_, so there!”
“You darling!” cried Tommy, his arms tightly round her. “I was determined to make you say it. I owe you something for the relentless way you’ve squashed me whenever I’ve tried to be sentimental.”
Tuppence raised her face to his. The taxi proceeded on its course round the north side of Regent’s Park.
“You haven’t really proposed now,” pointed out Tuppence. “But after listening to a rotten one like Julius’s, I’m inclined to let you off.”
“You won’t be able to get out of marrying me, so don’t you think it.”
“What fun it will be,” responded Tuppence. “Marriage is called a haven, and a crowning glory, and a state of bondage. But do you know what I think it is?”
“What?”
“A sport!”
“And a damned good sport too,” said Tommy.

original_source:
“THAT was a mighty good toast, Jane,” said Mr. Hersheimmer, as he and
his cousin were being driven back in the Rolls-Royce to the _Ritz_.

“The one to the joint venture?”

“No--the one to you. There isn’t another girl in the world who could
have carried it through as you did. You were just wonderful!”

Jane shook her head.

“I don’t feel wonderful. At heart I’m just tired and lonesome--and
longing for my own country.”

“That brings me to something I wanted to say. I heard the Ambassador
telling you his wife hoped you would come to them at the Embassy right
away. That’s good enough, but I’ve got another plan. Jane--I want you to
marry me! Don’t get scared and say no at once. You can’t love me right
away, of course, that’s impossible. But I’ve loved you from the very
moment I set eyes on your photo--and now I’ve seen you I’m simply crazy
about you! If you’ll only marry me, I won’t worry you any--you shall
take your own time. Maybe you’ll never come to love me, and if that’s
the case I’ll manage to set you free. But I want the right to look after
you, and take care of you.”

“That’s what I want,” said the girl wistfully. “Some one who’ll be good
to me. Oh, you don’t know how lonesome I feel!”

“Sure thing I do. Then I guess that’s all fixed up, and I’ll see the
archbishop about a special license to-morrow morning.”

“Oh, Julius!”

“Well, I don’t want to hustle you any, Jane, but there’s no sense in
waiting about. Don’t be scared--I shan’t expect you to love me all at
once.”

But a small hand was slipped into his.

“I love you now, Julius,” said Jane Finn. “I loved you that first moment
in the car when the bullet grazed your cheek....”

Five minutes later Jane murmured softly:

“I don’t know London very well, Julius, but is it such a very long way
from the _Savoy_ to the _Ritz?_”

“It depends how you go,” explained Julius unblushingly. “We’re going by
way of Regent’s Park!”

“Oh, Julius--what will the chauffeur think?”

“At the wages I pay him, he knows better than to do any independent
thinking. Why, Jane, the only reason I had the supper at the _Savoy_ was
so that I could drive you home. I didn’t see how I was ever going to
get hold of you alone. You and Tuppence have been sticking together
like Siamese twins. I guess another day of it would have driven me and
Beresford stark staring mad!”

“Oh. Is he----?”

“Of course he is. Head over ears.”

“I thought so,” said Jane thoughtfully.

“Why?”

“From all the things Tuppence didn’t say!”

“There you have me beat,” said Mr. Hersheimmer. But Jane only laughed.

In the meantime, the Young Adventurers were sitting bolt upright,
very stiff and ill at ease, in a taxi which, with a singular lack of
originality, was also returning to the _Ritz_ via Regent’s Park.

A terrible constraint seemed to have settled down between them. Without
quite knowing what had happened, everything seemed changed. They were
tongue-tied--paralysed. All the old _camaraderie_ was gone.

Tuppence could think of nothing to say.

Tommy was equally afflicted.

They sat very straight and forbore to look at each other.

At last Tuppence made a desperate effort.

“Rather fun, wasn’t it?”

“Rather.”

Another silence.

“I like Julius,” essayed Tuppence again.

Tommy was suddenly galvanized into life.

“You’re not going to marry him, do you hear?” he said dictatorially. “I
forbid it.”

“Oh!” said Tuppence meekly.

“Absolutely, you understand.”

“He doesn’t want to marry me--he really only asked me out of kindness.”

“That’s not very likely,” scoffed Tommy.

“It’s quite true. He’s head over ears in love with Jane. I expect he’s
proposing to her now.”

“She’ll do for him very nicely,” said Tommy condescendingly.

“Don’t you think she’s the most lovely creature you’ve ever seen?”

“Oh, I dare say.”

“But I suppose you prefer sterling worth,” said Tuppence demurely.

“I--oh, dash it all, Tuppence, you know!”

“I like your uncle, Tommy,” said Tuppence, hastily creating a diversion.
“By the way, what are you going to do, accept Mr. Carter’s offer of
a Government job, or accept Julius’s invitation and take a richly
remunerated post in America on his ranch?”

“I shall stick to the old ship, I think, though it’s awfully good of
Hersheimmer. But I feel you’d be more at home in London.”

“I don’t see where I come in.”

“I do,” said Tommy positively.

Tuppence stole a glance at him sideways.

“There’s the money, too,” she observed thoughtfully.

“What money?”

“We’re going to get a cheque each. Mr. Carter told me so.”

“Did you ask how much?” inquired Tommy sarcastically.

“Yes,” said Tuppence triumphantly. “But I shan’t tell you.”

“Tuppence, you are the limit!”

“It has been fun, hasn’t it, Tommy? I do hope we shall have lots more
adventures.”

“You’re insatiable, Tuppence. I’ve had quite enough adventures for the
present.”

“Well, shopping is almost as good,” said Tuppence dreamily. “Think of
buying old furniture, and bright carpets, and futurist silk curtains,
and a polished dining-table, and a divan with lots of cushions.”

“Hold hard,” said Tommy. “What’s all this for?”

“Possibly a house--but I think a flat.”

“Whose flat?”

“You think I mind saying it, but I don’t in the least! _Ours_, so
there!”

“You darling!” cried Tommy, his arms tightly round her. “I was
determined to make you say it. I owe you something for the relentless
way you’ve squashed me whenever I’ve tried to be sentimental.”

Tuppence raised her face to his. The taxi proceeded on its course round
the north side of Regent’s Park.

“You haven’t really proposed now,” pointed out Tuppence. “Not what our
grandmothers would call a proposal. But after listening to a rotten one
like Julius’s, I’m inclined to let you off.”

“You won’t be able to get out of marrying me, so don’t you think it.”

“What fun it will be,” responded Tuppence. “Marriage is called all sorts
of things, a haven, and a refuge, and a crowning glory, and a state of
bondage, and lots more. But do you know what I think it is?”

“What?”

“A sport!”

“And a damned good sport too,” said Tommy.

preservation_plan.book_context: Final coda after the treaty is burned and Mr. Brown (Sir James) is unmasked at the Savoy supper. The book has run a joint venture of Tommy and Tuppence that began with Tuppence scorning sentiment and planning to marry money. It also ran Julius's photograph-born infatuation with Jane, his businesslike proposal to Tuppence (which she declined because she loves Tommy), and Tommy's jealous outburst when he believed her dead. The chapter mirrors two couples in two cars both detouring via Regent's Park. It closes the 'adventure/sport' motif that opened in the Lyons' tea shop.
continuity_checks: Julius and Jane ride in the Rolls-Royce; Tommy and Tuppence ride in a taxi; both go via Regent's Park to the Ritz.
'Head over ears' is said first by Julius about Beresford, then echoed by Tuppence about Julius.
Carter offered the Government job and Julius the American ranch post. Do not swap them.
Tommy's uncle line (if kept) presupposes the Savoy chapter's Sir William reconciliation.
Tuppence, not Tommy, says 'Ours'. Tommy speaks the last line.

essential: Julius and Jane are driving back to the Ritz in the Rolls-Royce. He praises her toast and her courage. She says she feels tired, lonesome and homesick.

Julius proposes and mentions the Embassy invitation as the alternative. He has loved her since seeing her photo. He promises patience and to 'set you free' if she never loves him. He wants the right to look after her.
Keep Julius's hustling comedy: the special license 'to-morrow morning' right after promising not to hustle her.
Jane accepts with a declaration of present love, tied to the bullet grazing his cheek.

The Regent's Park detour joke: Jane asks if it is a long way from the Savoy to the Ritz, and Julius replies 'It depends how you go.' Julius admits he held the supper at the Savoy to get her alone, away from Tuppence. He confirms Beresford is 'head over ears'. Jane deduces this from what Tuppence didn't say.
Tommy and Tuppence sit stiff and tongue-tied in a taxi on the same route. Their old camaraderie has gone.
Tommy forbids Tuppence to marry Julius. She says Julius asked only out of kindness and loves Jane. Keep the 'sterling worth' tease and Tommy's flustered reply.
Futures: Tommy will 'stick to the old ship', meaning Carter's job, rather than Julius's ranch post, because she'd be at home in London. Keep 'I don't see where I come in' / 'I do'.
Money: Tuppence knows the size of their cheques but won't tell. This reprises her mercenary trait.
Tuppence's furnishing reverie leads to 'Ours'. Tommy embraces her and says he owes her for squashing his sentiment.
Tuppence remarks that this hasn't really been a proposal, though it beats Julius's 'rotten' one. Tommy says she won't get out of marrying him.
End on marriage as 'a sport', keeping her list of conventional names for marriage briefly and Tommy's closing line.
optional: Paragraph 16-17: the chauffeur's wages joke can be cut, but keep Julius's Savoy confession and the Siamese-twins line in condensed form.
Paragraphs 26-28 and 31-32: the beats of strained silence can collapse into one sentence.
Paragraphs 41-43: Tommy's condescending remarks on Jane can be trimmed to one line.
Paragraph 46: 'I like your uncle, Tommy' can be cut, but keep it framed as a diversion leading into the job question.
Paragraphs 54-56: the cheque exchange can be compressed to a single tease.
Paragraph 59: the furnishing list can be shortened to two or three items, but must still lead into 'flat' and 'Ours'.
Paragraph 68: the list of marriage descriptors can be shortened, but keep its contrast with 'A sport'.
risks: The 600-word target is tight given the dialogue-driven comedy. Favour compressing narration over cutting the punchlines.

preservation_plan.voice_profile: Brisk, comic third-person narration, mostly carried by quick dialogue. Christie's lightness depends on understatement and ironic narrative asides ('with a singular lack of originality'), speech tags that colour delivery (dictatorially, meekly, demurely, condescendingly, unblushingly), and clipped exchanges ending on a punchline. Julius speaks American slang (sure thing, hustle, I guess). Tommy is gruff and laconic. Tuppence is pert, mercenary and teasing, and covers feeling with banter. Sentiment is shown obliquely, through silence, evasion and jokes, never stated straight.
